post.title: Quirq iOS Device Loop
post.hook: A one-page iPhone app, built so every install can be traced to the change behind it.
post.summary: A minimal SwiftUI app showing the quirq mark, name and tagline, plus a build stamp, used to test a build-and-install loop driven by Claude. It is blocked until Xcode supports the iPhone 17 Pro.
post.writeup:
## What it is
quirq-ios is a one-page SwiftUI app: the quirq "q" mark, the name, the line "watch the work, not the meter", and a faint build stamp at the bottom. Colors and the mark come from the quirq site and its favicon.

## Why
The app itself is deliberately tiny. The real experiment is the device loop: Claude builds a signed copy with a bumped build number, installs it on a physical iPhone, and the stamp (`v0.1 (build) · date`) lets each install be matched to the change that produced it. Then you tell Claude what to change and repeat.

## How it works
The mark is drawn in code as a SwiftUI Shape: a ring, a stem and a rounded foot, combined with path union and subtraction inside a 100 x 132 design box. The build stamp reads the version and build number from the bundle info. Builds run through `xcodebuild` targeting the phone itself (so a free team can register it), then `xcrun devicectl device install app` pushes the result.

Setup is a one-time chore: add an Apple Account in Xcode, trust the cable connection, and enable Developer Mode on the phone. A free account's installs expire after 7 days.

## Findings
The loop hit a hard blocker, confirmed on 21 October 2026: Xcode 16.4 cannot use an iPhone 17 Pro. Its device support image covers chips up to the A18 Pro (`0x8140`), while the phone's A19 Pro is `0x8150`, so Xcode cannot mount the image, register the phone or build for it.

## Open questions
The fix is a newer Xcode, either via macOS 27.0.1 and Xcode 27, or macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 and Xcode 26.3. Until then the loop is untested end to end. The folder also holds a second, default Xcode template project with only placeholder tests.
